pageData.title: The Rashidun Caliphate
pageData.para1: The Rashidun Caliphate. When Muhammad died in 632 CE, he left no clear successor - and within thirty years his community had conquered an empire stretching from the Atlantic approaches to Central Asia. The Rashidun, the 'Rightly Guided' caliphs - Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, and Ali - were companions of the Prophet who ruled from Medina and Kufa, chosen by consultation rather than inherited by blood. Their caliphate (632-661) was Islam's first state, and the speed of what it did has few parallels in history.
pageData.para2: Abu Bakr's two-year reign (632-634) nearly saw it all collapse. Across Arabia, tribes declared their allegiance had ended with Muhammad; some withheld the zakat tax, others rallied to rival prophets like Musaylima. Abu Bakr's Ridda Wars - the 'wars of apostasy' - crushed the rebellion and welded Arabia into a single polity under Medina. It was the decisive act: an Arabian army unified under one command then turned outward, against a Byzantine Empire and a Sasanian Persia that had just bled each other white in a generation-long war.
pageData.para3: Under Umar (634-644) the conquests became a flood. Arab armies shattered the Byzantines at Yarmouk (636) and took Jerusalem (638); they destroyed Sasanian power at al-Qadisiyyah, captured the Persian capital Ctesiphon, and broke the last imperial resistance at Nihavand (642). Egypt fell by 642, and by Umar's death the caliphate held two-thirds of the Byzantine world and nearly all of Persia. Umar organized what the sword had won: garrison cities, stipends for the soldiers, pensions for the Prophet's companions - the institutions of a state, not just a raiding confederacy.
pageData.para4: The last two reigns brought triumph and tragedy together. Uthman (644-656) completed the conquest of Persia and pushed into North Africa and Armenia, but accusations of nepotism toward his Umayyad kinsmen ended with rebels besieging his house and murdering him. Ali (656-661), the Prophet's cousin and son-in-law, inherited a community at war with itself: the First Fitna pitted him against Muawiya, Uthman's kinsman and governor of Syria, until Ali's own assassination in 661 left Muawiya to found the Umayyad dynasty. The Rashidun era - elected caliphs ruling as first among the companions - was over, but its thirty years had changed the world permanently.

pageData.title: The Umayyad Caliphate
pageData.para1: The Umayyad Caliphate. The Umayyad Caliphate (661-750 CE) turned the young Islamic state into one of the largest empires the world has ever seen. Founded by Muawiya ibn Abi Sufyan, the long-serving governor of Syria who emerged victorious from Islam's first civil war, it moved the capital from Medina to Damascus and replaced the elected leadership of the Rashidun with something new: a hereditary dynasty, ruling an empire of millions - most of them not Arabs and not Muslims.
pageData.para2: The dynasty's early decades were stormy. Muawiya's son Yazid faced the revolt of Husayn, the Prophet's grandson, killed at Karbala in 680 - a wound in the community that has never healed. The Second Fitna that followed nearly destroyed the dynasty until Abd al-Malik (r. 685-705) reunified the empire by 692 and then rebuilt it: he Arabized the bureaucracy, replacing Greek and Persian with Arabic as the language of administration, minted the first distinctly Islamic coinage, and crowned his reign with the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem - the first great monument of Islamic architecture.
pageData.para3: Under Abd al-Malik's sons, above all al-Walid I, the conquests reached their astonishing peak. In a single year, 711, Umayyad armies crossed into Spain - toppling the Visigothic kingdom within a few years - and conquered Sindh in the Indus valley; in the east, others took Samarkand and Bukhara and pushed to the borders of China, while in the west the whole North African coast fell. At its height the caliphate stretched from the Atlantic to the Indus, perhaps 11 million square kilometers. It governed this vast, mostly Christian, Zoroastrian and Buddhist population with a light hand: the tolerated faiths paid the jizya tax and ran much of the civil service.
pageData.para4: But the empire devoured itself. Constant frontier warfare - including the great failed sieges of Constantinople - drained the treasury; Arab tribal rivalries tore the army apart; and the mawali, non-Arab converts who were Muslims yet treated as second-class citizens, provided the Abbasid revolution with its tinder. In 750 the Abbasids destroyed the dynasty at the Battle of the Zab and massacred the family. One prince, Abd al-Rahman I, escaped across Africa to Spain, where he founded the Emirate of Cordoba - so the Umayyad story continued for three more centuries, in the land where their conquests had reached farthest.

pageData.title: The Buyids
pageData.para1: The Buyids. The Buyid dynasty (934-1062) marks the moment the Abbasid caliphs lost control of their own empire. A family of Daylamite soldiers from the mountains south of the Caspian Sea, the three sons of Buya - Imad al-Dawla, Rukn al-Dawla, and Mu'izz al-Dawla - carved out principalities across western Iran in the 930s and 940s, and in 945 the youngest, Ahmad, marched into Baghdad itself. The Abbasid caliph stayed on his throne, but as a figurehead; real power now belonged to the Buyid amirs.
pageData.para2: The arrangement defined Middle Eastern politics for a century. The Buyids were Shia - first Zaydi, then Twelver - ruling over a majority-Sunni population and keeping the Sunni Abbasid caliph as a legitimizing ornament: he invested them with titles, they kept him under watch. Remarkably, they were tolerant rulers on both sides, supporting the caliph while patronizing Shia shrines and festivals. Historians call their era the 'Iranian Intermezzo' - the centuries between the Arab conquest and the Turkish Seljuk takeover when Iranian dynasties ruled Iran again.
pageData.para3: And they ruled as self-conscious Persians. The Buyids revived Sasanian royal traditions: some took the ancient title Shahanshah, 'King of Kings', and they carved inscriptions into the ruins of Persepolis, which they venerated as the work of the mythical king Jamshid. Under Adud al-Dawla (r. 949-983) the dynasty reached its height - from the borders of Syria to Khorasan - and he is remembered for building projects like the Band-e Amir dam and for a court that patronized poets, scientists, and historians. Arabic remained the language of administration, but New Persian literature flourished under Buyid protection.
pageData.para4: The dynasty never solved its central weakness: it was a family confederation, and after Adud al-Dawla's death the brothers and cousins fought over Fars, Ray, and Baghdad until the pieces were picked off one by one. The Ghaznavids and Kakuyids took the east; in 1055 the Seljuk sultan Tughril entered Baghdad, ending Buyid rule in Iraq; the last line in Fars held on until 1062. Their century, though, left a template - a Persian-Islamic synthesis of kingship, patronage, and tolerance - that the Seljuks and every later Iranian dynasty would build on.

pageData.title: The Seljuk Empire
pageData.para1: The Seljuk Empire. The Seljuk Empire (1037-1194) was the power that reunited the Islamic world - and the invasion that changed Anatolia forever. The Seljuks were Oghuz Turks, nomads from the steppes near the Aral Sea, who swept into Khorasan in the 1030s, shattered the Ghaznavids at Dandanaqan in 1040, and in 1055 entered Baghdad, where the Abbasid caliph - long a puppet of the Buyids - welcomed Tughril as sultan, the temporal sword of a now firmly Sunni restoration.
pageData.para2: Under Tughril's nephew Alp Arslan the empire turned west, annexing Armenia and Georgia and raiding deep into Byzantine Anatolia. The collision came at Manzikert in 1071, where Alp Arslan destroyed the Byzantine army and captured the emperor Romanos IV himself. It was one of history's decisive battles: Byzantine power in Anatolia never recovered, and within two decades Turkoman settlers and warlords had established principalities as far as the Aegean. The old heartland of Byzantium was becoming Turkey - and it was the shock of Manzikert and the Seljuk advance on Jerusalem that set the Crusades in motion a generation later.
pageData.para3: The empire's golden age came under Malik Shah I (r. 1072-1092) and his brilliant Persian vizier Nizam al-Mulk, who for all practical purposes ran the state - contemporaries called it 'the Nizam's state'. From the new capital at Isfahan they ruled from the borders of China to the Mediterranean. Nizam al-Mulk founded the Nizamiyya madrasas, the network of colleges that defined Sunni scholarship for centuries, and organized the iqta land-grant system that financed the army. Persian was the language of court and culture, Arabic of law and theology: the Turco-Persian synthesis that would shape Islamic civilization from India to Anatolia.
pageData.para4: The empire did not long survive its golden age. Malik Shah and Nizam al-Mulk both died in 1092 - the vizier assassinated, likely by the new Order of Assassins - and the succession struggles never really ended. The eastern half broke away under Ahmad Sanjar until the catastrophic defeat at Qatwan in 1141 by the Kara Khitai; the western sultans lingered until the Khwarazmians finished them in 1194. But the Seljuk world lived on in its offshoots - above all the Sultanate of Rum in Anatolia, which endured until 1308 - and in the institutions and culture they passed to their Ottoman heirs.

pageData.title: The Crusader States (1098-1291)
pageData.para1: The Crusader States, also called the Latin East or Outremer, were four territories founded in the Levant by the armies of the First Crusade: the County of Edessa (1098), the Principality of Antioch (1098), the Kingdom of Jerusalem (1099), and the County of Tripoli (1109). Three of them clung to a narrow coastal strip defended by castles such as Krak des Chevaliers, while Edessa lay inland on the frontier of the Syrian desert. Their founding was marked by mass killing. When Jerusalem fell on 15 July 1099, the crusaders slaughtered the city's Muslim and Jewish inhabitants. European chroniclers claimed tens of thousands of victims; the contemporary Muslim scholar Ibn al-Arabi put it at around 3,000 of the city's probable 30,000 residents; modern historians treat the higher numbers as exaggeration. Massacres of local people continued as the settlers imposed feudal rule, until they learned that holding the territory required the support of its diverse communities. The settlers, known locally as Franks, remained a small minority, outnumbered roughly five to one by Muslims, and lived among Greek Orthodox and Armenian Christians, Jews, Bedouin Arabs, and Muslims of various sects. A limited toleration developed, but these communities faced discriminatory laws and taxes, and almost all authority, secular and religious, stayed in Frankish hands.
pageData.para2: Violence stayed central to the states' history. After the crusaders captured Acre in July 1191, Richard I of England, angered by delays in the agreed ransom, ordered the entire surrendered Muslim garrison, 2,700 men, marched outside the walls and executed in view of Saladin's army. Saladin struck back by killing most of his Christian prisoners. Trade made the states rich: Acre became one of the great Mediterranean ports, charging duties of 4 to 25 percent on goods moving between east and west, and the Kingdom of Jerusalem minted its own gold coinage, something only Sicily in Europe managed at the time. Saladin's victory at Hattin in 1187 cost the states Jerusalem, but they fought on: the Third Crusade regained the coast, Acre became the new capital, and Jerusalem itself was regained through Emperor Frederick II's diplomacy in 1229, only to be lost again in 1244. The end came in 1291, when Acre fell to the Mamluks; the states' mainland lands were absorbed into the Mamluk Sultanate, and the Latin East survived only as a refuge on Cyprus.

pageData.title: The Fatimids
pageData.para1: The Fatimids. The Fatimid Caliphate (909-1171) was the great Shia rival to the Sunni caliphs of Baghdad - an empire that began with a revolutionary movement in North Africa and ended up ruling from one of the greatest cities of the medieval world, Cairo, which the Fatimids themselves founded. The dynasty claimed descent from Fatima, the Prophet Muhammad's daughter, and her husband Ali: to their Ismaili Shia followers, the Fatimid caliph was not merely a ruler but the Imam, the divinely guided leader of all Muslims.
pageData.para2: The movement began in the early 900s, when the Ismaili missionary Abu Abdallah won over the Kutama Berbers of what is now Algeria and overthrew the Aghlabid rulers of Ifriqiya (Tunisia) in 909. From concealment in far-off Sijilmasa came Abdallah al-Mahdi, accepted as the long-awaited Imam and first caliph. For sixty years the Fatimids ruled from Tunisia, fighting off Abbasid agents, Umayyad Spain, and their own Berber rebels, while their missionaries - the da'is - quietly built networks of supporters across the Islamic east.
pageData.para3: In 969 the general Jawhar conquered Egypt almost without a fight, and the Fatimids built their new capital beside the Nile: al-Qahira, 'the Victorious' - Cairo. Under al-Mu'izz, al-Aziz, and the long, strange reign of al-Hakim, Egypt became the richest state in the Mediterranean, its fleets dominating the sea lanes and its merchants linking the Indian Ocean trade to Europe. They founded al-Azhar mosque and its academy, still today a great center of Islamic learning, and presided over a cosmopolitan court of Sunni officials, Christian administrators, and Jewish merchants - the caliphate never managed to convert its own mostly-Sunni population to Ismailism, and mostly did not try.
pageData.para4: The long reign of al-Mustansir (1036-1094) brought decay: army factions fought in the streets of Cairo, famine struck, and the empire lost Syria to the Seljuk Turks and then Jerusalem to the Crusaders in 1099. Viziers like Badr al-Jamali and his son propped up the shrinking state for another century, but in 1171 the last caliph's own vizier - the young Saladin - quietly abolished the dynasty, returned Egypt to the Sunni fold and the Abbasid name, and founded his own Ayyubid sultanate on the Fatimid inheritance.

pageData.title: The Ilkhanate
pageData.para1: The Ilkhanate. The Ilkhanate (1256-1335) was the Mongol Empire's Middle Eastern wing - the state founded by Hulegu, grandson of Genghis Khan, and the regime that destroyed the Abbasid Caliphate after five centuries. Sent west by his brother the Great Khan Möngke with a fifth of the entire Mongol army, Hulegu first annihilated the Nizari Ismaili state of the Assassins in their mountain fortresses (1256), then, in 1258, took Baghdad: the city was sacked, the last Abbasid caliph al-Musta'sim was executed, and the classical age of the caliphate ended in a single week.
pageData.para2: Hulegu pushed on into Syria, taking Aleppo and briefly reaching Gaza, but the Mongol tide met its first lasting check in 1260: recalled east by Möngke's death, he left a small force in Palestine that the Mamluks of Egypt destroyed at Ain Jalut - the battle that fixed the Mongol frontier at the Euphrates. The Ilkhanate - 'subordinate khanate', in theory answerable to the Great Khan in China - settled down to rule Iran, Iraq, Azerbaijan, and Anatolia from its capitals at Maragheh and Tabriz, fighting the Mamluks in the west and its Mongol cousins of the Golden Horde in the north.
pageData.para3: The early Ilkhans were Buddhists ruling a Muslim population, tolerant of Christians and Jews, and the conversion of Ghazan in 1295 changed everything: Islam became the state religion, and the Mongol rulers of Iran became Iranian Muslim sultans. Ghazan and his brother Öljeitü presided over a brilliant revival - the vizier Rashid al-Din wrote the Jami al-Tawarikh, the first true history of the world; the Maragheh observatory, built for the astronomer Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, was the most advanced on earth; and Tabriz, astride the trade routes, grew fabulously rich.
pageData.para4: The state could not outlive its founders' line. Abu Sa'id, the last effective Ilkhan, died in 1335 without an heir - with the Black Death already ravaging the realm - and the khanate shattered into a dozen local dynasties. But its century left deep marks: the concept of 'Iranzamin', the Land of Iran, as a unified kingdom was revived under Mongol rule, Persian historiography and miniature painting reached new heights in its service, and the way was opened for Timur and, eventually, the Safavids.

pageData.title: The Timurid Empire
pageData.para1: The Timurid Empire. The Timurid Empire (1370-1507) was the last great nomadic conquest empire of Central Asia - the creation of Timur, known to the West as Tamerlane, a warlord of the Turkicized Mongol Barlas tribe who built an empire from Delhi to Anatolia in thirty-five years of unbroken campaigning. Unable to claim descent from Genghis Khan, Timur married into the dynasty, took the title Gurkani - 'son-in-law' - and ruled through puppet khans while holding all real power himself from his magnificent capital at Samarkand.
pageData.para2: Timur saw himself as the restorer of the Mongol Empire, and his campaigns revived its methods as well as its borders. He crushed his former protégé Tokhtamysh and the Golden Horde, sacked Baghdad and Damascus - where the historian Ibn Khaldun met him in 1401 and found him both terrifying and brilliant - and in 1398 descended on Delhi, leaving the city a ruin from which the Delhi Sultanate never recovered. His most consequential victory came at Ankara in 1402, where he defeated and captured the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I, throwing the rising Ottoman state into a decade of civil war and buying Constantinople another fifty years. He died in 1405, marching to conquer China.
pageData.para3: His successors traded conquest for culture, and the result was the Timurid Renaissance. Timur's son Shah Rukh (r. 1405-1447) ruled from Herat, which he made one of the most refined courts in the Islamic world, a center of miniature painting, calligraphy, and Persian poetry. Shah Rukh's son Ulugh Beg was himself an astronomer: his observatory at Samarkand produced star tables of unmatched precision for their era. A century later, the court of Husayn Bayqara at Herat gave the world the painter Bihzad and the poet Jami - the final flowering of the classical Persian tradition.
pageData.para4: The empire's political story was briefer than its cultural one. The Timurids lost Persia to the Aq Qoyunlu Turkomans by 1469, and in 1500-1507 the Uzbeks under Shaybani Khan took Samarkand and Herat. But the dynasty had one more act: the young Timurid prince Babur, driven from his Central Asian homeland, turned east and in 1526 conquered Delhi - founding the Mughal Empire, which would rule India for three centuries. Through the Mughals, Timur's bloodline and his Persianate culture outlasted his empire by four hundred years.

pageData.title: The Eastern Roman Empire (The Byzantines)
pageData.para1: The Eastern Roman Empire (The Byzantines). The Byzantine Empire was the Roman Empire - continuing without interruption for a thousand years after Rome itself fell. Its citizens never called themselves Byzantines; they were Romans, their state Rhomania, their capital the New Rome that Constantine the Great founded on the site of Byzantium in 330. 'Byzantine Empire' is a modern label for what was, to its people and its neighbors alike, simply the Empire - Greek-speaking, Christian, and ruled from Constantinople, the greatest city of the medieval world.
pageData.para2: Its first age of glory came under Justinian I (r. 527-565), who rewrote Roman law in the Corpus Juris Civilis - the foundation of Europe's legal tradition - rebuilt the Hagia Sophia, and sent his general Belisarius to reconquer North Africa and Italy from the Vandal and Ostrogothic kingdoms. But plague in the 540s and grinding wars with Persia followed, and in the 630s-640s the Arab conquests stripped away the Levant and Egypt, costing the empire as much as three-quarters of its revenue. The empire that survived was smaller and Greek rather than Latin, reorganized for defense through the theme system - troops assigned to defend specific provinces - behind the Theodosian Walls of Constantinople, built under Theodosius II.
pageData.para3: The Macedonian dynasty, founded when Basil I seized the throne in 867, brought a two-century renaissance. Soldier-emperors like Nikephoros II and John Tzimiskes recovered Cilicia and Antioch, and under Basil II (r. 976-1025) - conqueror of Bulgaria after the decisive victory at Kleidion in 1014 - the empire stretched from the Danube and southern Italy to the Euphrates, its medieval peak. Then came Manzikert: in 1071 the Seljuk Turks destroyed the Byzantine field army, and Anatolia, the empire's heartland and recruiting ground, was opened to Turkish settlement. The Komnenian emperors partially restored the empire, but it was now one power among several.
pageData.para4: The deathblow came from the West: in 1204 the knights of the Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople and carved the empire into competing Latin realms and Greek successor states. The empire recovered its capital in 1261 under Michael VIII, but as a shadow of itself - a regional power watching the Ottoman Turks annex its remaining territories through the 14th and 15th centuries. In 1453 Constantinople finally fell to the Ottomans, and with it perished Constantine XI, the last Roman emperor. Rome's two-thousand-year story had ended.

pageData.title: The Sultanate of Rum
pageData.para1: The Sultanate of Rum. The Sultanate of Rum (1077-1308) was the Turkish state that made Anatolia Turkish. Founded in the aftermath of Manzikert by Suleiman ibn Qutalmish, a prince of the Seljuk family, it took its name from what everyone in the Islamic world called the land: Rum - 'Rome', the old Byzantine empire. Ruling first from Nicaea and then from Konya (ancient Iconium) from 1097, the sultanate held central Anatolia for two and a half centuries, the years in which the peninsula's language, faith, and identity were transformed.
pageData.para2: The sultanate weathered the Crusades - its armies bore the brunt of the Crusader columns crossing Anatolia - and emerged stronger. Under Kaykhusraw I, who took the Mediterranean harbor of Antalya in 1207, and his son Kaykaus I, who captured Sinop and made the Empire of Trebizond a vassal in 1214, and above all under Kayqubad I (1220-1237), the sultanate reached its height: Anatolia's coasts on both seas, trade from Iran and Central Asia flowing through a famous network of caravanserais - fortified inns a day's journey apart - and wealth enough to absorb the rival Turkish principalities of the east.
pageData.para3: Konya in these years was one of the Islamic world's most cultured courts. Though its founders were Oghuz Turkish warriors, the sultanate's high culture was Persian - the language of its court, its literature, and its administration - blended with the Turkish of its soldiers and the Greek of its subjects into a distinctive Anatolian civilization, enriched by Persian scholars fleeing the Mongol advance. The sultans endowed the mosques, madrasas, and caravanserais whose stonework still defines the cities of central Turkey.
pageData.para4: The end came from the steppe: in 1243 the Mongol army crushed Sultan Kaykhusraw II at Köse Dağ, and Rum became a vassal of the Ilkhanate, its sultans reduced to appointees and then figureheads. As Mongol control loosened, the sultanate dissolved into a patchwork of beyliks - small Turkish principalities - until the last Seljuk sultan, Mesud II, was murdered in 1308. One of those beyliks, a tiny marcher state in the northwest ruled by the house of Osman, would reunite Anatolia and far more: the Ottoman Empire was the Sultanate of Rum's true heir, inheriting its land, its institutions, and even its respected coinage.

pageData.title: Kingdom of Georgia
pageData.para1: Kingdom of Georgia. The Kingdom of Georgia (c. 1008-1490) was the great Christian power of the Caucasus - a mountain kingdom that, for one shining century, dominated the whole region from the Black Sea to the borders of Iran. It was born in 1008, when Bagrat III of the Bagrationi dynasty inherited the thrones of Abkhazia and Iberia and united the Georgian lands under one crown for the first time, after centuries of division between rival kingdoms and Arab and Byzantine overlords.
pageData.para2: The kingdom's first century was a struggle for survival: wars with Byzantium under Basil II cost Georgia its western lands, and from the 1060s the Seljuk Turks overran much of the country. Salvation came with David IV, 'the Builder' (r. 1089-1125), who crushed the feudal lords, stopped paying tribute to the Seljuks, and rebuilt the army with Kipchak steppe warriors settled in exchange for service. In 1121, when the Muslim powers of the region declared holy war, David destroyed their coalition at the Battle of Didgori - the victory that ended Turkish hegemony in the Caucasus. He took Tbilisi the same year and made it his capital, pushed on to capture Ani and Shirvan, and founded the Gelati Academy, famed in its day as 'a new Hellas'.
pageData.para3: The Golden Age crowned by his great-granddaughter, Queen Tamar (r. 1184-1213) - who ruled in her own right with the royal title 'King of Kings' - made Georgia the pre-eminent state of the Christian East, its tributaries stretching from eastern Europe to Anatolia and the northern frontiers of Iran. Tamar not only shielded her empire from Turkish invasion but crushed internal revolts, including two by her own former husband. In 1204, as the Crusaders sacked Constantinople, her armies founded the Empire of Trebizond on the Black Sea as a friendly Georgian-backed Byzantine successor state, and Georgia's wealth endowed monasteries from Bulgaria to Jerusalem.
pageData.para4: The Mongols broke it. The invasions of the 13th century reduced Georgia to vassalage, and though George V 'the Brilliant' expelled the Mongol garrisons and restored its sovereignty and prosperity by the 1340s, the Black Death - said to have carried off half the population - and then Timur's devastating invasions at the century's end ruined the land. Isolated by the Ottoman conquest of Byzantium and Trebizond, the kingdom fractured into the rival kingdoms of Kartli, Kakheti, and Imereti by 1490. Georgia's golden century was over - but the memory of David and Tamar has anchored Georgian national identity ever since.

pageData.title: The Fragmentation of Anatolia
pageData.para1: The Fragmentation of Anatolia. After the Seljuk victory at Manzikert in 1071 threw Anatolia open, the peninsula filled with Turkish principalities - beyliks, territories ruled by beys, the Turkish equivalent of dukes. The first wave were frontier lordships, the uç beys or 'marcher lords' the Seljuk sultans of Rum planted on the Byzantine border to wage holy war and hold the marches: Danishmends, Saltukids, Artuqids, and others, nominally loyal to Konya but kings in all but name on their own ground.
pageData.para2: The second and greater wave came when the Seljuk center collapsed. The Mongol victory at Köse Dağ in 1243 reduced the Sultanate of Rum to an Ilkhanid dependency, and as Mongol power in Anatolia faded after 1300, the beys declared themselves sovereign outright. By the early 14th century the map of Anatolia was a patchwork of some two dozen principalities: the Karamanids and Germiyanids in the center, the sea-roving beyliks of the Aegean coast - Karasi, Saruhan, Aydin, Mentese, Teke - whose ghazi warriors raided the Christian shipping lanes, the Candar dynasty on the Black Sea, and in the far northwest, pressed against the Byzantine frontier around the town of Sogut, one small beylik among many: the Osmanoglu, the house of Osman.
pageData.para3: The beyliks fought everyone - the retreating Byzantines, the Genoese trading colonies, the crusading Knights, and above all each other. Yet this fractured frontier world drew constant reinforcement: ghazi warriors from Persia and Turkestan, and refugees fleeing the Mongol invasions, streamed into Anatolia, and the ghazi ethos - holy war on the frontier, rewarded with land and glory - gave the beyliks their restless energy.
pageData.para4: The consolidation was the Ottomans' story. Osman's heirs expanded at Byzantine expense along the Sea of Marmara, absorbed the neighboring beylik of Karasi, and crossed into Europe in 1354; by the late 14th century they had bought, married, or conquered most of their rivals. Timur's crushing of the Ottomans at Ankara in 1402 briefly restored the old beyliks, but within a generation the house of Osman had swallowed them again - and the fragmented Anatolia of the beys became the heartland of the Ottoman Empire.

pageData.title: The Göktürk Khaganates
pageData.para1: The Göktürk Khaganates. The Göktürks - the 'Celestial Turks' - were the first people in history to build an empire under the name Turk. In 552, Bumin Qaghan of the Ashina clan, whose people had worked metal for the Rouran Khaganate in the Altai Mountains, overthrew his masters and founded the First Turkic Khaganate. Within a generation his descendants ruled the Mongolian Plateau and much of Central Asia, straddling the Silk Road between China, Sasanian Persia, and Byzantium.
pageData.para2: The khaganate was a new kind of state: a tribal confederation bound to the Ashina clan, whose authority came from Tengri, the sky god - the khagan ruled because heaven had granted him qut, divine fortune. Its people were multi-ethnic; whatever the Ashina themselves originally spoke, their empire spread Turkic speech and a common steppe culture across Eurasia. 'Turk' itself began as the name of this ruling people alone - the Göktürks did not count the Uyghurs or Kyrgyz as Turks - before becoming the label of a whole world of peoples.
pageData.para3: The empire's curse was division. Civil war among the khagans split it into Eastern and Western khaganates, and China's Tang dynasty exploited the weakness: in 630 Emperor Taizong's armies crushed the Eastern khaganate at the Battle of Yinshan and captured its ruler, and the eastern Turks spent fifty years as Tang subjects. But in 682 Ilterish Qaghan and his chancellor Tonyukuk raised the revolt that founded the Second Turkic Khaganate, restoring steppe independence for another sixty years - the age of Bilge Khagan and his brother Kul Tigin.
pageData.para4: That restored empire left us its own voice: the Orkhon inscriptions, memorial steles raised in the Orkhon valley to Kul Tigin and the chancellor Tonyukuk, carved in the Old Turkic runic script - the first steppe empire to tell its story in its own words. In 744 the Uyghurs, allied with the Tang, destroyed the last khaganate and took the Mongolian Plateau - but the Göktürk model of a Turkic empire would echo down to the Seljuks and Ottomans.

pageData.title: The Uyghur Khaganate
pageData.para1: The Uyghur Khaganate. The Uyghur Khaganate (744-840) ruled the steppe for a century between the Göktürks and the Mongols - and it broke the steppe's oldest rule, for the Uyghurs built cities. Calling themselves the Toquz Oghuz, the Nine Tribes, they rose in 744 when a Uyghur-Karluk alliance destroyed the Basmyls who had toppled the Second Göktürk Khaganate; the next year they killed the last Göktürk khagan and sent his head to the Tang emperor. From their capital at Ordu-Baliq on the Orkhon - a walled city on the open steppe - the Uyghur khagans ruled, in the words of the Tang histories, 'the entire territory of the ancient Xiongnu'.
pageData.para2: The Uyghurs built their empire on an unusual foundation: not raiding China but rescuing it. When the An Lushan rebellion nearly destroyed the Tang dynasty in 755, it was Uyghur cavalry that retook the capitals Chang'an and Luoyang - and the Uyghurs collected their price in silk: tens of thousands of rolls a year, a horse trade fixed at forty rolls of silk per horse, marriage alliances with Tang princesses, and 'guest' status for Uyghurs in China. When the Tang retreated from Central Asia after their defeat by the Arabs at Talas in 751, the Uyghurs were left the dominant power of the Silk Road, and Sogdian merchants flocked to their court.
pageData.para3: In 762 the khagan Bögü, campaigning in China, encountered Manichaean priests - and converted. It was an astonishing choice: a steppe empire adopting, as its state religion, the Persian faith of light and darkness, a religion of books and merchants rather than warriors. The khaganate's official religion became Manichaeism, practiced alongside Tengrism, Buddhism, and Nestorian Christianity - an empire of unusual religious diversity even by steppe standards.
pageData.para4: The end came with terrible speed. Famine, epidemic, and a killing winter in 839-840 gutted the herds the empire lived on, and in 840 the Yenisei Kyrgyz - invited in by a rebellious Uyghur minister - swept down with 80,000 horsemen, sacked and burned Ordu-Baliq, and destroyed the khaganate in a single campaign. The Uyghurs fled south and west as refugees; in the oases of Gansu and the Tarim Basin they built new states, the Gansu Uyghur Kingdom and the Kingdom of Qocho, that carried Uyghur culture on for centuries.

pageData.title: The Khazar Khaganate
pageData.para1: The Khazar Khaganate. The Khazar Khaganate (c. 650-965) was the great trading empire of the western steppe - and home to one of the most remarkable religious choices in medieval history: its ruling elite converted to Judaism. The Khazars, a Turkic tribal confederation, emerged as the most powerful state from the breakup of the Western Turkic Khaganate, dominating the grasslands from the Volga-Don steppes to the Crimea and the northern Caucasus.
pageData.para2: Khazaria's power was geography. Astride the routes between Eastern Europe, the Islamic world, and China, it commanded the western marches of the Silk Road, and its capital Atil, at the Volga delta, grew rich taxing the trade of three continents. For three centuries the khagans stood as the indispensable buffer of the early medieval world: first as Byzantium's proxy against Sasanian Persia, then as the barrier between the Umayyad and Abbasid caliphates and the endless steppe. Its peoples were as mixed as its trade: Turkic tribes, pagans, Muslims, Christians, and Jews, ruled with notable tolerance.
pageData.para3: Then, in the 8th century, the Khazar court did something no other state has done before or since: the khagan Bulan and his elite adopted Rabbinic Judaism - a third faith, belonging to neither of the great powers pressing on Khazaria, Christian Byzantium and the Islamic caliphate. How far the conversion spread beyond the ruling class remains genuinely uncertain; the sources are sparse, and the state stayed multireligious. The khagan Joseph's famous letter to Hasdai ibn Shaprut, the Jewish minister of Cordoba, remains our best window into this Jewish steppe kingdom, which corresponded in Hebrew while speaking a Turkic tongue.
pageData.para4: Khazaria's end came when the balance shifted against it. Around 900 Byzantium, no longer needing its buffer, encouraged new enemies against it, and by 969 Sviatoslav of Kiev stormed and destroyed Atil; the khaganate disintegrated by the mid-11th century, its peoples absorbed by Cumans, Rus', and others. One caution for the modern reader: the 19th-century theory that most Ashkenazi Jews descend from the Khazars is a myth - linguistic and genetic studies do not support it, most scholars reject it, and it has often been put to antisemitic uses. The real Khazars need no myth: a Jewish court ruling the Silk Road's western gate is remarkable enough.

pageData.title: The Mongol Empire
pageData.para1: The Mongol Empire. The Mongol Empire was the largest contiguous land empire in all of history - at its height stretching from the Sea of Japan to Eastern Europe, from Siberia to the borders of India. It was the creation of one man: Temüjin, born around 1162, abandoned by his tribe on the steppe after his father was poisoned, who fought his way from fugitive to master of Mongolia. In 1206 a great assembly, the kurultai, proclaimed him Genghis Khan, ruler of the 'Great Mongol Nation'.
pageData.para2: Genghis did not just unite the tribes; he abolished them. In what the historian Timothy May calls a 'social revolution', he broke up the old tribal loyalties and reforged the steppe into a decimal army - units of ten, a hundred, a thousand - commanded by ninety-five chosen officers, some of humble birth, loyal to him alone. This machine, disciplined and mobile, campaigned against the Jin dynasty and the Western Xia in northern China and destroyed the Khwarazmian Empire; when Genghis died in 1227 his empire already stretched from the Pacific to the Caspian, twice the size of Rome's at its height. Under his son Ögedei the conquests rolled on: the Jin dynasty finished by 1234, Goryeo Korea reduced to a client state, Kievan Rus' overrun, and in 1241 victories at Legnica and on the Sajo River carried Mongol armies into Poland and Hungary.
pageData.para3: The empire Genghis founded was more than a war machine. Under the Pax Mongolica, the 'Mongol Peace', the routes from the Pacific to the Mediterranean lay under one power's protection for the first time: merchants, missionaries, technologies, commodities, and ideologies crossed Eurasia as never before. But the succession law never matched the conquests. Genghis's grandsons fought over the inheritance, and after Möngke Khan died in 1259, the Toluid Civil War (1260-1264) between his brothers Kublai and Ariq Böke broke the empire's unity for good.
pageData.para4: By Kublai Khan's death in 1294 the empire had become four sovereign khanates: the Golden Horde in Russia, the Chagatai Khanate in Central Asia, the Ilkhanate in Iran, and Kublai's own Yuan dynasty in China. They fell in turn - the Ilkhanate by 1353, the Yuan to the Ming in 1368, the Golden Horde by the end of the 15th century - while Chagatai's heirs lasted, in one corner or another, into the 1700s. In barely a century and a half the Mongols had conquered half the known world and lost it, and in the process rewired it: the Silk Road age they opened, and the devastation they left, shaped everything that came after.

pageData.title: The Golden Horde
pageData.para1: The Golden Horde. The Golden Horde - the Ulus of Jochi, its rulers called it - was the northwestern quarter of the Mongol Empire, and for two centuries the master of Russia. It grew from the lands assigned to Jochi, Genghis Khan's eldest son, but its real founder was Jochi's son Batu, whose great western campaign with the general Subutai conquered Volga Bulgaria and then the Russian principalities - Ryazan fell in December 1237, Kiev was sacked in the winter of 1240-41 - before his armies smashed the Poles and Hungarians at Legnica and Mohi in 1241. From his new capital at Sarai on the lower Volga, Batu and his heirs ruled from Siberia to the Danube - and collected tribute from every Russian prince.
pageData.para2: The Russian principalities kept their own rulers and their Orthodox faith; the Horde demanded submission and tribute, and its word was law: the princes of Rus' traveled to Sarai to acknowledge the khan's supremacy and renew their patents of rule. The khans themselves changed faith and language: Batu's brother Berke, enthroned in 1257, was a convert to Islam, and under Özbeg Khan (1312-1341) - who made Islam the state religion - the Horde reached its peak, its Mongol ruling class by then thoroughly Turkicized, speaking the Kipchak tongue of their steppe subjects.
pageData.para3: Sarai itself was a cosmopolitan capital where the khans licensed churches as well as mosques. But the mid-14th century brought the 'Great Troubles' (1359-1381), a generation of civil war between rival khans. Tokhtamysh briefly reunited the Horde (1381-1395), only for Timur's invasion of 1396 to shatter it for good: the khanate broke into smaller khanates that declined steadily in power.
pageData.para4: The wreck broke into successor khanates - Kazan, Astrakhan, Crimea, the Nogai and Uzbek hordes - while the shrunken 'Great Horde' on the Volga clung to its claims until 1480, when the famous 'stand on the Ugra River' ended with the khan's army simply turning away: the traditional end of the 'Tatar yoke' over Russia. In 1502 the Crimean khan sacked Sarai itself. Yet the Horde's shadow was long: the Crimean Khanate, its last heir, survived until 1783 - five and a half centuries after Batu rode west.

pageData.title: The Gupta Empire
pageData.para1: The Gupta Empire. The Gupta Empire (c. 320-550) ruled northern India during what many historians call India's Golden Age - a label some modern scholars dispute, but one the age's achievements make hard to resist. Founded by Chandragupta I, crowned in 320 at Pataliputra, the dynasty rose from a local Magadha kingdom - its position strengthened by his marriage to the Licchavi princess Kumaradevi - to an empire spanning most of the northern subcontinent.
pageData.para2: Its greatest conqueror, Samudragupta (c. 335-375), is known to us largely through his own court poet's panegyric, the Allahabad Pillar inscription, which claims he uprooted eight kings of the north, defeated twelve rulers of the south, and received tribute from the forest tribes and the frontier kingdoms from Nepal to Assam - claims modern historians read with care, since the inscription dressed diplomacy as submission. He performed the ancient horse sacrifice of imperial sovereignty and minted gold coins showing him playing the veena: a 'king of poets' as well as a conqueror.
pageData.para3: Under Samudragupta's son Chandragupta II and grandson Kumaragupta I, the empire enjoyed its Pax Gupta. The age's culture set the standards of Indian art and thought for a thousand years: the Mahabharata and Ramayana took their classical written form, the Puranas were compiled, Kalidasa wrote the works that remain Sanskrit literature's summit, while Aryabhata, Varahamihira, and Vatsyayana made their lasting advancements in scholarship. Hindu in allegiance - the Guptas patronized Brahmanical ritual - the empire was tolerant of other faiths, and its art 'set standards of form and taste that determined the whole subsequent course of art, not only in India but far beyond her borders'.
pageData.para4: The end came from the steppe. From the late 5th century the Huna peoples - the Kidarite and Alchon Huns of Central Asia - broke through the northwest frontier, and the empire's own feudatories carved away its territory; by around 550 the Guptas were gone and India fragmented again into regional kingdoms. But the template endured: for later Indians, the Gupta age remained the classical standard of kingship, art, and learning - the age against which all later Indian civilization measured itself.

pageData.title: The Harsha Empire
pageData.para1: The Harsha Empire. Harshavardhana (r. 606-647) was the last great emperor of ancient northern India - a philosopher-king whose court we can see with unusual clarity, because both a Chinese pilgrim and a Sanskrit poet wrote about him from life. When the Gupta Empire fell in the mid-6th century, northern India shattered into small kingdoms; from the minor kingdom of Thanesar, Harsha - who had already fought the Alchon Huns - was crowned Maharajadhiraja, 'king of great kings', at an assembly of the northern states in April 606, and welded the region from Punjab to central India into one empire, ruled from his capital at Kannauj.
pageData.para2: Harsha's empire was Indian kingship at its most attractive. The Chinese Buddhist pilgrim Xuanzang, who visited his court and knew him as Shiladitya, praised his justice and generosity: a king who banned the slaughter of animals for food, built monasteries and thousands of stupas along the Ganges, maintained hospices for travelers and the poor on the highways, and held a great charitable assembly every five years where he gave away his accumulated wealth. The poet Banabhatta's Harshacharita records the reign from inside - the capital's defensive wall, moat, and palace with its two-storied white mansion. Harsha himself is widely believed to have written three Sanskrit plays that survive.
pageData.para3: His reach had one hard limit: the Narmada River. When Harsha marched south to conquer the Deccan, the Chalukya emperor Pulakeshin II defeated him at the Battle of Narmada, and the river stayed the empire's southern boundary for the rest of his reign. His religious policy was the opposite of dogmatic: personally drawn to Buddhism while born into the Shaiva tradition, he patronized both, presiding over festivals where he and his vassal kings performed daily rituals before a golden statue of the Buddha.
pageData.para4: Harsha died in 647, and the empire he had assembled outlived him only as a name: Kannauj passed to lesser kings, and northern India fragmented again. His forty-one years were a brief golden interlude between the Guptas and the Rajput age, but between Xuanzang's travelogue and Bana's biography, we know it better than almost any reign in ancient India.

pageData.title: The Rajput Kingdoms
pageData.para1: The Rajput Kingdoms. From the seventh century onward, northern and western India came to be ruled by a constellation of warrior dynasties later known as the Rajputs - a word from the Sanskrit rajaputra, "son of a king." Scholars note that most Rajput clans actually rose from peasant or pastoral communities: families that won land and renown by the sword and then claimed royal descent. By the 12th century the great clans - the Gurjara-Pratiharas of Kannauj, the Chauhans of Ajmer, the Tomaras of Delhi, the Solankis of Gujarat, the Paramaras of Malwa, the Gahadavalas, the Chandelas of Khajuraho, and the Sisodias of Mewar - held the subcontinent's heartland as rival fortressed kingdoms, bound by a shared code of honor and horsemanship.
pageData.para2: The Rajput kingdoms stood first against the invaders from the northwest. Rajput rulers repelled the early Arab invasions that followed the conquest of Sindh, holding them at the borders of Rajasthan. In 1025 Mahmud of Ghazni smashed through to sack the great temple of Somnath - its Solanki ruler Bhimdev fled his capital - though the fortresses of Gwalior and Kalinjar held out against him. Then in 1191 Prithviraj Chauhan led a coalition of Rajput kings that defeated Muhammad of Ghor at Taraori; a year later Ghor returned with an army of mounted archers and crushed the Rajput host on the same field. Prithviraj was captured and executed, and from his ruin rose the Delhi Sultanate.
pageData.para3: Yet the Rajputs were never conquered in spirit. From their desert forts - Chittor, Ranthambor, Jalore - they fought the sultans of Delhi for centuries: Alauddin Khalji had to sack Chittor and Ranthambor to break them, and within a generation Rana Hammir defeated a Tughluq army at Singoli in 1336 and recovered Rajasthan. In the 15th century Rana Kumbha of Mewar beat the sultans of Malwa and Gujarat alike, and his grandson Rana Sanga made Mewar one of the greatest powers in northern India, defeating three sultanates before falling to Babur's Mughals at Khanwa - Babur himself called Sanga, with Krishnadevaraya, the greatest Hindu king of the age.
pageData.para4: With the Mughals, most Rajput states moved from war to alliance: Akbar built his empire with Rajput support, sealing it with marriage alliances - seventeen between his family and Rajput houses - and his son Jahangir and grandson Shah Jahan were both born of Rajput mothers. Proud Mewar alone refused to give daughters to the Mughals, and Rana Pratap's long defiance of Akbar made him the enduring Rajput icon of independence. When Aurangzeb abandoned his ancestors' tolerance, Rajput revolts from the 1680s helped tear the Mughal empire apart. The Rajputs' legacy is written across Rajasthan in its great hill forts - and in an epic, the Prithviraj Raso, that gave a scattered warrior people a single heroic memory.

pageData.title: Pala Empire
pageData.para1: Pala Empire. The Pala Empire (750-1161) was the last great Buddhist imperial power in India - and one of history's more unusual origin stories. When Gopala was elected king by the chiefs of Gauda in the mid-8th century, he was, as an Arabic source puts it, 'not a king of noble origin'; Bengal had endured generations of anarchy, and the regional chiefs chose a ruler to end it. From that improvised beginning, the Palas built an empire covering Bengal and Bihar that, at its early-9th-century zenith under Dharmapala and Devapala, dominated northern India from the Gangetic Plain to the Vindhya Range.
pageData.para2: The Palas fought and negotiated their way through the great 'tripartite struggle' for Kannauj against the Gurjara-Pratiharas and the Rashtrakutas, fielding a famous corps of war elephants and a navy that worked the Bay of Bengal. But their deepest power was cultural. Devout Buddhists ruling a largely Hindu population - their inscriptions and images show generous patronage of Shiva and Vishnu too - they made their court the stronghold of late Indian Buddhism: they raised the great monasteries of Somapura Mahavihara and Odantapuri and patronized the universities of Nalanda and Vikramashila, then at their world-famous height.
pageData.para3: Pala influence traveled with its monks and merchants. The scholar Atisa Dipankara carried Bengal's Buddhism to Tibet, where the Pala legacy still shapes Tibetan Buddhism today; the empire maintained relations with Srivijaya in Indonesia, with Tibet, and with the Abbasid Caliphate - contacts along which Islam first reached Bengal. At home the Pala centuries were a golden age of Bengali art: the sculpture, bronzes, and manuscript paintings of Pala workshops, and the Charyapada songs of its tantric Buddhist poets, among the earliest texts in the eastern Indian languages.
pageData.para4: The empire's later centuries were a long defense: Mahipala I fought off the Chola invasions from the south, and Ramapala, the last strong Pala emperor, briefly revived its power. But the Varendra rebellion of the 11th century exposed how dependent the Palas had become on their feudatories, and in the 12th century the Hindu Sena dynasty drove them from Bengal itself. When the last Pala, Govindapala, disappears from record in 1161, the age of Buddhist imperial power in India ended with him.

pageData.title: The Chola Empire
pageData.para1: The Chola Empire. The Chola Empire (848-1279) was south India's greatest maritime power - a Tamil dynasty that held peninsular India for three centuries and ruled the waves of the Bay of Bengal. The Cholas were ancient: they appear in Ashoka's edicts of the 3rd century BCE and in the Sangam poems as one of Tamilakam's Three Crowned Kings. But the empire began in 848, when Vijayalaya, scion of an old Chola line serving the Pallavas, seized his chance and restored the dynasty from its heartland in the rich Kaveri river valley.
pageData.para2: The imperial age opened with Rajaraja I, under whom the Cholas unified peninsular India south of the Tungabhadra as one state - a unity they held from 907 to 1215. His son Rajendra I outdid him: he marched an army north to the Ganges, completing the conquest of Rajarata in Sri Lanka on the way - styling himself Gangaikonda Chola and building a new capital, Gangaikonda Cholapuram, to prove it - and in 1025 sent the Chola fleet across the Bay of Bengal to raid the empire of Srivijaya in Sumatra, an expedition from which Srivijaya never fully recovered. Chola embassies reached China in 1016, 1033, and 1077.
pageData.para3: The Cholas built in proportion to their ambitions. Rajaraja's Brihadisvara temple at Thanjavur - its domed sikhara resting on a single block of granite weighing some 80 tons - remains a masterpiece of Dravidian architecture, the centerpiece of a temple-building age that covered the Tamil country with stone monuments to the dynasty's power and piety.
pageData.para4: The empire endured, through constant wars with the Chalukyas, the Pandyas, and the Sinhalese, into the 13th century; the last great king, Kulothunga III, held it together until 1215, after which the resurgent Pandyas absorbed it, and by 1279 the Chola name passed from power. Their legacy is south India's own: the Tamil country held as a single state for three centuries, the great temple cities of the Kaveri valley, and a seafaring tradition that carried Tamil commerce and culture across the Bay of Bengal to Southeast Asia.

pageData.title: The Delhi Sultanate
pageData.para1: The Delhi Sultanate. The Delhi Sultanate (1206-1526) was the first great Muslim empire of India - for more than three centuries a state based in Delhi that stretched over large parts of the subcontinent. Its history falls into five dynasties: the Mamluk (1206-1290), the Khalji (1290-1320), the Tughlaq (1320-1414), the Sayyid (1414-1451), and the Lodi (1451-1526). It was founded in the ruins of the Rajput order: after Muhammad of Ghor routed Prithviraj Chauhan's confederacy near Tarain in 1192, his Turkic slave-generals divided his Indian conquests, and one of them, Qutb ud-Din Aibak, declared himself sultan at Delhi in 1206.
pageData.para2: Aibak began the Qutb Minar and the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque, and his son-in-law and successor Iltutmish finished the great tower while consolidating the fragile sultanate - conquering Multan and Bengal and holding the throne for a quarter-century. After his death came the age of the Corps of Forty, the kingmaker nobles, and of Razia Sultana (r. 1236-1240), one of the very few women to rule an Islamic state, until the stern Balban (1266-1287) broke the nobles and restored royal authority. In 1290 the Khaljis seized the throne in revolution.
pageData.para3: Under Ala ud-Din Khalji, who seized the throne by murder in 1296, the sultanate became the subcontinent's terror and its shield: his armies conquered Gujarat, Malwa, and the Rajput forts, his general Malik Kafur raided deep into the south - carrying back the fabled Koh-i-Noor among the Warangal loot - and Delhi stood as one of the few powers in Asia to repel the Mongols. Ala ud-Din ruled as a tyrant, raising agricultural taxes from a fifth to half the harvest, fixing prices in state-controlled markets, and slaughtering suspected opponents with their families. Under the Tughlaqs the sultanate reached its greatest extent: Muhammad bin Tughluq briefly held most of the subcontinent and moved his capital south to Daulatabad, before overreach and revolt scattered his empire.
pageData.para4: The blow that broke the sultanate came from outside: Timur's sack of Delhi in December 1398. Out of the wreckage rose rival powers - the Hindu Vijayanagara Empire and the Rajput kingdom of Mewar, the independent Bengal and Bahmani sultanates - while the shrunken Sayyid and Lodi dynasties held Delhi until 1526, when the Timurid prince Babur destroyed Sultan Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat and founded the Mughal Empire. Yet the sultanate's three centuries changed India permanently: it drew the subcontinent into the wider Islamic world, gave it the Hindustani language and the first masterpieces of Indo-Islamic architecture, and filled its cities with the scholars, mystics, and artisans who had fled the Mongol storm in the west.

pageData.title: The Khmer Empire
pageData.para1: The Khmer Empire. The Khmer Empire (802-1431) was the greatest power of mainland Southeast Asia - a civilization of kings and hydraulic cities centered on what is now northern Cambodia, which at its height ruled or vassalized most of the mainland as far north as southern China. Its people called their land Kambuja. The empire is conventionally dated from 802, when the prince Jayavarman II declared himself chakravartin - universal ruler - on the sacred mountain of Phnom Kulen, founding the line of god-kings that would build Angkor.
pageData.para2: The early kings laid Angkor's foundations: Indravarman I built at Hariharalaya, and his son Yasovarman I founded Yasodharapura, the first city of the Angkor area, raising its temple on the hill of Phnom Bakheng and digging the East Baray, a reservoir over seven kilometers long. This was the empire's secret: mastery of water. The barays and canals that stored the monsoon and fed the rice fields made Angkor's prosperity - and, as satellite imaging has revealed, made its capital region the most extensive pre-industrial urban complex in the world, with a population of some 700,000 to 900,000 at its 13th-century peak, one of the most populous cities of the medieval world.
pageData.para3: The twelfth century brought the empire's most famous monument: under Suryavarman II (r. 1113-1150), who united the empire internally, Angkor Wat rose over thirty-seven years as a temple-mountain dedicated to Vishnu - still the largest religious monument of the pre-modern world. But the century ended in near-disaster: in 1177 a Cham fleet sailed up the Tonle Sap lake, sacked the capital, and killed the king. Salvation came with Jayavarman VII (r. 1181-1218), the last great king of Angkor, who crushed the Chams, then rebuilt his capital as Angkor Thom with the many-faced towers of the Bayon at its center. A follower of Mahayana Buddhism, he filled the empire with temples - Ta Prohm for his mother, Preah Khan for his father - and with roads, rest-houses, and 102 hospitals.
pageData.para4: After Jayavarman VII the great building slowed; Theravada Buddhism, arriving from Sri Lanka in the 13th century, gradually displaced the old court religions. The empire's end is still debated: researchers have found that violent swings between monsoon flood and drought damaged the hydraulic system on which Angkor depended, and people drifted away from the great cities. In 1431 Angkor fell to the Siamese kingdom of Ayutthaya, and the court withdrew south. But the stones remain: Angkor Wat, the Bayon's serene faces, and a hundred temples still testify to the power, wealth, and artistry of Kambuja.

pageData.title: The Pagan Kingdom
pageData.para1: The Pagan Kingdom. The Pagan Kingdom (1044-1287) was the first empire to unify the lands that are now Myanmar - and for 250 years its capital on the Irrawaddy was the beating heart of Burmese civilization. The kingdom grew from a small 9th-century settlement of the Mranma people - the ancestors of today's Bamar - who had migrated into the Irrawaddy valley and fused with the older Pyu culture they found there. Pagan's 250-year rule laid the foundations of Burmese language and culture and made Theravada Buddhism the faith of mainland Southeast Asia.
pageData.para2: The empire's founder was Anawrahta, who came to the throne in 1044 and spent his first decade turning the parched lands of central Myanmar into a rice granary, building weirs and canals around the Kyaukse district - the irrigated heartland that would be the economic key of every Burmese state after him. Then he unified the valley: by the 1070s Pagan held Upper and Lower Burma, and tradition credits his 1057 conquest of the Mon kingdom of Thaton with bringing back Buddhist scriptures and the Mon script, from which the Burmese alphabet was made. Just as important was Anawrahta's own conversion to Theravada Buddhism: his patronage gave the school a refuge just as it was retreating elsewhere in Asia, and in 1071 Pagan helped restart the Theravada order in Ceylon itself.
pageData.para3: Under Anawrahta's successors - Kyanzittha, Alaungsithu, and their heirs - Pagan reached its golden age. Alaungsithu (r. 1112-1167) standardized weights, measures, and administration, while Burmese finally emerged from the shadow of Mon and Pyu to become the kingdom's written language. And the kings built: over the centuries Pagan's rulers raised more than 10,000 Buddhist temples on the plain of Bagan, of which over 2,000 still stand - one of the great archaeological landscapes on earth. In the 12th and 13th centuries, Pagan stood alongside the Khmer Empire as one of the two great powers of mainland Southeast Asia.
pageData.para4: The temples were also the kingdom's undoing. As kings and nobles gave ever more tax-free land to the Buddhist order, the crown's revenues shrank until by the 1280s it could no longer hold the loyalty of its courtiers and soldiers. When Mongol armies invaded in 1277, the hollow kingdom could not stand: Pagan fell in 1287, and its collapse opened 250 years of fragmentation in Myanmar. But everything it created endured - the Burmese language, the Theravada faith, and the spires of Bagan, still rising from the Irrawaddy plain.

pageData.title: The Champa Kingdoms
pageData.para1: The Champa Kingdoms. Champa (192-1832) was the remarkable maritime civilization of the Vietnamese coast - a chain of Austronesian Cham kingdoms that for over sixteen centuries stood where the trade routes of China met those of India. It began in 192 CE, when a local official broke away from Chinese rule to found the kingdom known to Chinese records as Linyi. Scholars now debate how unified Champa ever was: at times a single kingdom, at times a federation of river-mouth polities, each commanding its own harbor on the long coast.
pageData.para2: In the 4th century, wars with neighboring Funan brought Indian culture flooding into Cham society: Sanskrit became the language of inscriptions, Shaivism the religion of kings. The first king known from inscriptions, Bhadravarman (r. 380-413), founded the sanctuary of My Son, where he raised a linga joining his own name with Shiva's - and for centuries the red-brick towers of My Son and the Po Nagar temple at Nha Trang stood as the holy places of a Hindu kingdom. The Chams were the great sailors of Southeast Asia: their ports linked the spice trade from the Persian Gulf to South China, and their apogee came in the 9th and 10th centuries, when Cham merchants and sailors were known from the ports of India and Java to the Philippines.
pageData.para3: Champa's history was written in war with its landward neighbors. With the Khmer Empire the rivalry was epic and mutual: in 1177 a Cham fleet sailed up the Mekong and sacked Angkor itself, and the Khmer king Jayavarman VII answered by conquering Champa a generation later. But the fatal pressure came from the north, from Dai Viet. Century by century the Vietnamese pushed south; in 1471 they stormed Vijaya, Champa's capital, and the old kingdom was broken, surviving only as the rump state of Panduranga until Vietnam's Nguyen dynasty annexed it in 1832.
pageData.para4: The Cham people survived their kingdom. Cham-speaking communities still live in Vietnam and Cambodia - some Muslim, a faith that spread among the Chams from the 10th century, some keeping the old Hindu rites, one of the last living links to the Indianized age of Southeast Asia. Their language traveled too: the Acehnese of northern Sumatra speak a tongue descended from Chamic. And the towers of My Son and the old port of Hoi An, both World Heritage sites, keep the memory of the sailor-kings of Champa.

pageData.title: Srivijaya Empire
pageData.para1: The Srivijaya Empire. Srivijaya (c. 671-1025) was the first great power of maritime Southeast Asia - a Malay Buddhist empire based at Palembang on Sumatra that for three and a half centuries dominated the western archipelago and the straits through which all trade between India and China had to pass. Its wealth was the wealth of the sea lanes: a prestige-goods economy built on controlling, taxing, and protecting the booming commerce of the region, with trade agreements nurtured with China from the Tang to the Song dynasty.
pageData.para2: Srivijaya was also a holy land of Buddhism. When the Chinese monk Yijing stopped at Palembang in 671, he found a thriving center of Buddhist learning where monks prepared for the journey to India; for four centuries the empire was one of the great centers for the expansion of Buddhism, maintaining religious and cultural links with the Pala kingdom of Bengal and even with the Islamic Caliphate. Its oldest voice survives in stone: the Kedukan Bukit inscription of 682, found near Palembang, records the king's sacred journey to found the empire's fortune.
pageData.para3: Historians once pictured Srivijaya as a pure thalassocracy ruling through its fleets; newer research sees a land-based kingdom whose navy existed to project land power and coerce trading ships into its ports. Either way, the straits were its lifeline - and when that lifeline was cut, the empire died. In 1025 the Chola Empire of south India, Srivijaya's great commercial rival, launched devastating raids on its ports across the straits. The kingdom may never have recovered: though Chinese sources kept naming a 'Sanfoqi' in the region, the center of power had passed, and the age of Srivijaya was over.
pageData.para4: So complete was its fall that Srivijaya was simply forgotten - even in Palembang itself, no one remembered the empire until the French scholar George Coedes resurrected it from Chinese records and Old Malay inscriptions in 1918. Today it stands revealed as the missing first chapter of Indonesian history: the first polity to dominate western maritime Southeast Asia, and the proof that the archipelago's seas could carry an empire.

pageData.title: Majapahit Empire
pageData.para1: The Majapahit Empire. Majapahit (1293-1527) was the last and greatest of the Hindu-Buddhist empires of Indonesia - a Javanese thalassocracy whose court poem, the Nagarakretagama of 1365, counted 98 tributary states from Sumatra to New Guinea, an extent no Indonesian state had ever claimed before. It was born in a double betrayal: in 1292 a Mongol Yuan fleet landed in Java to punish its king, and the prince Raden Wijaya allied with the invaders to destroy his usurper, then turned on the Mongols and drove them into the sea. From that victory he founded Majapahit, named for the bitter maja fruit of the forest where he built his capital at Trowulan.
pageData.para2: The empire's golden age came in the 14th century under Queen Tribhuwana and her son Hayam Wuruk (r. 1350s-1389), and above all under their great prime minister Gajah Mada, who at his inauguration swore the famous Palapa oath - that he would taste no rest until the whole archipelago was united under Majapahit. He nearly kept it: Bali fell in 1343, and Majapahit's fleets carried Javanese power across the islands, while the visiting friar Odoric of Pordenone found the court rich in cloves, nutmeg, and spices. Historians still debate how tight Majapahit's grip on its far tributaries really was - but none doubt it was the archipelago's center of power, trade, and culture.
pageData.para3: Majapahit was Hindu-Buddhist in faith - Shaivism and Buddhism side by side - and its red-brick capital of Trowulan, laced with canals, was one of the great cities of Southeast Asia. Its court produced the Nagarakretagama, an Old Javanese epic that remains our fullest picture of a classical Indonesian kingdom.
pageData.para4: The empire's fall was slow, then sudden. A civil war (1404-1406) weakened its hold on the vassal states, and as Islam spread along the trade routes, the empire slowly declined. In 1527 the rising Sultanate of Demak invaded and Majapahit collapsed - a fall that opened the age of Islamic kingdoms in Java, while Bali kept the old Hindu-Buddhist culture alive to this day. The fall of Majapahit closed the age of Hindu-Buddhist empires in Java - and opened the age of the Islamic sultanates of Indonesia.

pageData.title: Tang Dynasty
pageData.para1: The Tang Dynasty. The Tang dynasty (618-907) is remembered as China's golden age - a high point of Chinese civilization when the empire was the largest, richest, and most cosmopolitan state on earth. The dynasty was founded in 618 by Li Yuan, Duke of Tang, out of the collapse of the short-lived Sui; under his son Taizong (r. 626-649) - who seized the throne in the Xuanwu Gate Incident - and a succession of strong emperors, Tang armies pushed deeper into Inner Asia than even the Han had done, garrisoning the Silk Road and drawing tribute from kingdoms across Asia.
pageData.para2: The Tang capital Chang'an (modern Xi'an) was for much of the dynasty the most populous city in the world - a true metropolis where Persian merchants, Sogdian traders, Nestorian Christians, Manichaeans, Zoroastrians, and Muslims all worshipped and traded. The empire's population grew from some 50 million to an estimated 80 million. Tang government was run by scholar-officials recruited through standardized examinations, and Tang culture was the school of East Asia: Japan and Korea drew deeply on its culture, institutions, and letters.
pageData.para3: It was also the greatest age of Chinese poetry - Li Bai and Du Fu, the two most famous poets in Chinese history, were Tang men - and the age that saw woodblock printing develop, while Buddhism reached its Chinese peak before Emperor Wuzong's suppression in the 840s. Between 690 and 705 the dynasty was even interrupted by Wu Zetian, the only woman in Chinese history to rule as emperor in her own name.
pageData.para4: The turning point was the An Lushan rebellion (755-763), which devastated the north and permanently weakened the throne. Real power drained to the jiedushi, the regional military governors; agrarian rebellions tore the 9th century apart; and in 907 the last Tang emperor abdicated, opening the half-century of division known as the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms. But the Tang ideal - a unified, examination-governed, culturally confident China - became the standard every later dynasty measured itself against.

pageData.title: Song Dynasty
pageData.para1: The Song Dynasty. The Song dynasty (960-1279) ruled China during one of the most inventive eras in human history. Founded in 960 by Emperor Taizu, a general who ended the chaos of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms, the Song never matched the Tang's military reach - but it surpassed every dynasty before it in wealth, technology, and learning. China's population doubled to some 90 million, cities swelled, and the economy of 12th-century China dwarfed that of contemporary Europe.
pageData.para2: The Song age was an age of firsts: the world's first government-issued paper money, China's first permanent standing navy, the first surviving records of the gunpowder formula and gunpowder weapons - fire arrows, bombs, and the fire lance - the first use of the compass to find true north at sea, the pound lock for canals, and great astronomical clocks. Expanded rice cultivation with early-ripening strains fed the boom; printing spread books and learning; the examination system made the scholar-official the ruler of China.
pageData.para3: Yet the Song lived under siege. It never controlled the northern steppe and fought long wars with the Khitan Liao, the Tangut Western Xia, and then the Jurchen Jin - who in 1127 captured the capital Kaifeng and the emperor himself in the Jingkang catastrophe. The dynasty survived south of the Yangtze: the Southern Song, ruled from Lin'an (modern Hangzhou), remained a rich and populous state on its productive southern lands for another century and a half.
pageData.para4: The end came with the Mongols. After destroying the Jin in 1234, they turned south; Kublai Khan proclaimed the Yuan dynasty in 1271, took Lin'an in 1276, and annihilated the last Song loyalists at the naval Battle of Yamen in 1279. China was unified again - but under foreign rule. The Song legacy is subtler and perhaps greater: the commercial revolution, the printed book, the scholar's China, and technologies - gunpowder, compass, paper money - that would remake the world.

pageData.title: The Western Xia, Liao, & Jin Dynasties
pageData.para1: The Western Xia, Liao, and Jin Dynasties. Between the fall of the Tang and the rise of the Mongols, northern China was ruled not by Chinese dynasties but by three great conquest empires of steppe peoples: the Khitan Liao, the Tangut Western Xia, and the Jurchen Jin. Each blended nomadic power with Chinese government, and together they held the north for three centuries while the Song ruled the south.
pageData.para2: The first were the Khitans, a nomadic people of the northeast. In 907 their leader Abaoji became khagan; in 916 he took the title of emperor and founded the Liao dynasty (916-1125). The Liao created a remarkable dual state: a Northern Administration ruling the steppe tribes in the old nomadic way, and a Southern Establishment governing the settled Chinese population on Tang models, with its own Khitan scripts invented for the purpose. In 1005 the Chanyuan Treaty settled peace with the Song on equal terms. So dominant were the Khitans that their name - Khitai - became the word for China itself across Central Asia and Russia, reaching Europe as 'Cathay.'
pageData.para3: To the west, the Tanguts - a people of the northwest borderlands - proclaimed the Western Xia (1038-1227), ruling a million square kilometers of north-central China from their capital at Xingqing (modern Yinchuan). Buddhist and Confucian by turns, they created their own intricate script and held off both Song and Liao for two centuries. Their end was terrible: the Western Xia was annihilated by the Mongols in 1227, its records and architecture so thoroughly destroyed that its history was nearly lost until 20th-century scholarship recovered it.
pageData.para4: The third conquest came from the Jurchens, subject tribes of the Liao who rebelled under Aguda, who founded the Jin dynasty in 1115. The Jin destroyed their Liao overlords in 1125 - the Liao remnant fleeing west to found the Qara Khitai in Central Asia - then broke their Song allies, capturing Kaifeng, two emperors, and the entire northern heartland in the Jingkang catastrophe of 1127. The Jin ruled north China for over a century, from Manchuria to the Huai River, until the Mongols ground them down and took their last refuge at Caizhou in 1234. The steppe's three empires had proven that nomads could rule China; the Mongols were about to prove they could rule all of it.

pageData.title: The Yuan Dynasty
pageData.para1: The Yuan Dynasty. The Yuan dynasty (1271-1368) was China's first empire under foreign rule - the moment when the heirs of Genghis Khan ceased to be merely conquerors of China and became its emperors. In 1271 Kublai Khan, grandson of Genghis and Great Khan of the Mongol Empire, proclaimed the 'Great Yuan' in the Chinese style, taking the name from the I Ching and claiming the Mandate of Heaven and the succession of China's dynasties. In 1279 his forces destroyed the last Song resistance at the naval Battle of Yamen, and for the first time in history a non-Han dynasty ruled all of China proper.
pageData.para2: Kublai (r. 1260-1294) built a new capital at Dadu - modern Beijing - with a summer capital at Shangdu in the steppe. The Yuan empire was, in name, the supreme khanate of the Mongol world: the western khans formally recognized the Yuan emperor's supremacy in 1304, though in practice each khanate went its own way. The dynasty governed a vast multi-ethnic state, kept Mongolian written in the new 'Phags-pa script alongside Chinese, and circulated paper money across the empire.
pageData.para3: The Yuan century left deep marks on China: Beijing's career as the national capital began at Dadu, and the Pax Mongolica's open roads brought unprecedented contact between China and the world of Islam and Europe. Yet Mongol rule never fully took root. The emperors after Kublai grew weaker, and the dynasty's century closed in flood, famine, and rebellion: the Red Turban revolts that began in 1351 devoured the south, and in 1368 the rebel leader Zhu Yuanzhang drove the court from Dadu and proclaimed the Ming dynasty.
pageData.para4: The Yuan story did not quite end there: the Genghisid rulers retreated to the Mongolian plateau and ruled on as the 'Northern Yuan' until 1635. But in Chinese history, 1368 closed a unique chapter - the era when the steppe ruled the sown, and the world's largest land empire had its heart on the site of Beijing.

pageData.title: Nara, Heian, and Kamakura Japan
pageData.para1: Nara, Heian, and Kamakura Japan. Medieval Japan's story is told in three ages, each named for its seat of power: the Nara period (710-794), when Japan built itself on the Chinese model; the Heian period (794-1185), when it turned inward to create a culture all its own; and the Kamakura period (1185-1333), when the samurai seized the state. Together they transformed Japan from a student of China into a civilization with its own unmistakable voice.
pageData.para2: The Nara period opened in 710 when Empress Genmei established Japan's first permanent capital at Heijo-kyo (modern Nara), a city laid out on the grid of the Tang capital Chang'an. Everything Chinese was the model: Chinese writing, Chinese law codes, Chinese schools of Buddhism. The court commissioned Japan's first histories, the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, to glorify the imperial line, and its poets compiled the Man'yoshu, the great early anthology of Japanese verse.
pageData.para3: In 794 Emperor Kanmu moved the capital to Heian-kyo - Kyoto, which would remain the imperial capital for a thousand years - and the long Heian age began. Real power passed to the Fujiwara clan, who married their daughters to emperors and ruled as regents, while at court a refined aristocratic culture flowered: the new hiragana and katakana scripts freed Japanese from Chinese, and court women wrote the masterpieces of the age - Sei Shonagon's Pillow Book and Murasaki Shikibu's Tale of Genji. Buddhism took Japanese forms in the Tendai and Shingon sects of Saicho and Kukai. But beyond the capital, great estates slipped from imperial control, and the warrior class - the samurai - grew strong. In 1156 the warrior Taira no Kiyomori seized power; in the Genpei War that followed, the Taira were annihilated at the naval battle of Dan-no-ura in 1185.
pageData.para4: The victor, Minamoto no Yoritomo, did not abolish the throne - he simply ruled beside it. Taking the title of shogun in 1192, he governed Japan from Kamakura while the emperor reigned as figurehead in Kyoto: the shogunate, Japan's warrior government, had begun, and it would last nearly seven centuries. The Hojo clan soon ruled as regents for puppet shoguns; under them Japan survived the Jokyu War of 1221 and, above all, Kublai Khan's two Mongol invasions in 1274 and 1281 - both shattered by the typhoons Japan remembered as the kamikaze, the 'divine wind.' The age saw Zen, Pure Land, and Nichiren Buddhism take root among warriors and commoners. In 1333 Emperor Go-Daigo briefly overthrew the shogunate in the Kenmu Restoration, but the samurai order was irreversible: the Ashikaga shoguns followed in 1336, and warrior rule defined Japan until the 19th century.

pageData.title: Goryeo Kingdom
pageData.para1: The Goryeo Kingdom. Goryeo (918-1392) was the kingdom that gave Korea its name - the state that unified the peninsula and welded the old identities of Goguryeo, Baekje, and Silla into a single Korean nation. It was founded in 918 by the general Wang Kon, known as Taejo, during the chaos of the Later Three Kingdoms; by 936 he had peacefully absorbed Silla, conquered Later Baekje, and welcomed the fleeing ruling class of Balhae - achieving what Korean historians call the first true national unification. From his capital at Gaegyeong (modern Kaesong), his dynasty ruled for nearly five centuries.
pageData.para2: Goryeo's golden age, lasting into the early 12th century, was one of the brilliant civilizations of East Asia. Buddhism, the state religion, reached its highest influence in Korean history - the capital alone held 70 temples. Goryeo's merchants traded with Song China and even Arabia; its celadon pottery, perfected with the inlaid sanggam technique, was praised in China itself; and its reverence for learning produced the Tripitaka Koreana, the complete Buddhist canon carved on 81,258 wooden printing blocks - still preserved at Haeinsa temple and called by UNESCO one of the most important collections of Buddhist texts in the world. In the early 13th century, Goryeo craftsmen were printing books with movable metal type - two centuries before Gutenberg.
pageData.para3: The kingdom's later centuries were harder. From 1170 military dictators ruled behind the throne, and from 1231 came the Mongol invasions: Goryeo resisted for nearly 30 years from its island refuge on Ganghwa before suing for peace in 1259 and becoming a 'son-in-law state' of the Yuan dynasty (1270-1356). Yet even in vassalage the kingdom endured and recovered its independence as Mongol power waned.
pageData.para4: The end came in 1392, when the general Yi Seonggye - sent to invade Ming China in 1388 - turned his army around at the border, seized the throne, and founded the Joseon dynasty that would rule Korea into the modern age. But Goryeo's legacy is Korea itself: the nation's name, its unified identity, its celadon, its Buddhist canon, and a printing tradition that led the world.
